industrialization

/in-dus-tree-uh-luh-ZAY-shun/ - seven beats, stress on ZAY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Industrialization is the transformation of an economy from farm and hand labor to machine-driven factory production — a shift that remakes work, towns, and daily life together.

Industrialization reached the valley as sound before anything else: the mill whistle at six, where for two centuries there had been only church bells.

Example

In 1830 the parish rolls listed weavers, wheelwrights, and eleven kinds of smith; by 1870 they listed 'operatives.' Industrialization had moved through the county like weather — looms gathered into one brick mill, cottages emptied toward the mill towns, and a farmer's son could earn more in the foundry by seventeen than his father cleared in a year of harvests.

Industrialization is the name for that economy-wide remaking: production reorganizing around machines and factories, and work, towns, and daily hours reorganizing around production. The scale is the point. When one print shop buys a motorized press, that is mechanization; when a county's looms, forges, and fields all reorganize around the factory, the era itself has changed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

urbanization: Urbanization is industrialization's traveling companion — people massing into cities — but the two can part ways: a capital can swell with clerks and courtiers and never build a factory. Industrialization is about how things are produced, not where people crowd.

modernization: Modernization swaps old for new on any axis at all — dress, law, plumbing, schooling — and says nothing in particular about machines. Industrialization is one specific engine of it: production moving into machine-driven factories.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

agrarianism: an economy and way of life organized around farming

handcraft: goods made one at a time by skilled hands

Where it sits · how completely machines remake the work

mechanization → industrialization → automation

mechanization vs. industrialization: Mechanization is the milder change: machines take over a single task in a single workplace — one mill's looms, one cannery's line — while industrialization reorganizes a whole economy's production around the factory.

automation vs. industrialization: Automation pushes further than industrialization — industrialization gathers workers around the machines, while automation removes the workers from the loop entirely, the line running with no hands on it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — industri: diligence, hard work (Latin industria)

Suffix — -al: relating to

Suffix — -ization: the process of making

Put it together: Industri- (diligence) + -al (relating to) + -ization (the process of making) = the process of organizing an economy around industry. Latin industria named hard work itself — a virtue, not a sector; the factories borrowed the word centuries later, and the diligence came first.

Use the root in a new word: industrious: Two industrious summers paid for the pickup truck, and Salome never let her brothers forget which of them had stayed home.

Root Check

Word Choice

historical / economic

Industrialization is the historian's word for the whole transformation — factories, railways, mill towns, the shape of the working day — so keep it off single gadgets and single shops. Mechanization is one task passing to machines; urbanization is the crowding the factories draw; automation is the hands leaving the loop. On the SAT it anchors history and social-science passages, and the arguments are as often about its costs — hours, smoke, childhoods — as about its output.
